sn7.21:1.2: A Saṅgārava of Sāvatthī appears in a number of discourses, and his spiritual progression can be traced. Here he practices purification in water, and (apparently later) asked the Buddha about sacrifice ([an3.60]()). He further asked how hymns are remembered ([sn46.55](), [an5.193]()). In all these discourses he was said to have gone for refuge at the end. Finally he asks the more meaningful spiritual question about the near shore and far shore ([an10.117](), [an10.169]()). It is possible that the teenage “student” (_māṇava_) Saṅgārava living at Caṇḍalakappa ([mn100]()) graduated and moved to nearby Sāvatthī where he became known as the “brahmin” Saṅgārava. This would only make sense, however, if we disregard the statements on going for refuge, as he clearly followed the Brahmanical path for quite some time.
sn7.21:2.7: This is a very precise and clear statement of the pre-Buddhist quasi-physical understanding of good and evil. Such practices, which are detailed further in the Jatakas, clearly relate to magical thinking. Evidently such quasi-material thinking was shared between the Brahmins (at least some of them) and the Jains.
